excerpt: async with session.post(url, params=params) as response:
param: n/a (fires on every call, not caller-triggered)
sink: aiohttp ClientSession.post(url, params=params) where params includes {"api_key": api_key, ...}
why: api_key (SKYWORK_API_KEY / default "DEFAULT_KEY") is placed in aiohttp's params=, which aiohttp appends to the URL query string even on a POST -- the same construction is repeated identically across all 5 generate_* tools. A secret in the URL query string is routinely captured by web server access logs, reverse-proxy logs, and any request logging middleware, unlike a value sent in an Authorization header or JSON body. Fires unconditionally on every call regardless of what the caller supplies, so it is a design flaw rather than a caller-exploitable input-handling bug -- filed Tier B per the same 'fires on every call, no caller malice needed' reasoning as the mandatory-layer precedent for this class of finding.

sink: httpx.AsyncClient().get(url) inside fetch_url(), called on every result["link"] returned by the Serper search API
why: library is checked against a fixed allowlist (docs_urls), but query is caller-controlled free text concatenated as f"site:{docs_urls[library]} {query}" into the Serper search request. Google-style 'site:' search restriction is a soft text filter, not an enforced API-level domain constraint, and can be widened with additional search operators in query (e.g. an 'OR site:...' clause) to influence which links come back. Critically, once results come back, fetch_url() performs a server-side GET on result["link"] with zero check that the link's host actually matches docs_urls[library] -- there is no allowlist at the point of use at all, only the soft one on the outgoing query text. This is the same shape as an unvalidated-redirect-through-third-party-data SSRF: the caller doesn't supply a URL directly, but does control the search query that determines which URL gets fetched server-side, and nothing validates the result before fetching it.
contract: Search the latest docs for a given query and library. Supports langchain, openai, and llama-index.

why: This tool's entire advertised purpose is executing a shell command, and it fails closed by default: ALLOWED_COMMANDS is empty unless the operator sets it, so with no explicit configuration allowedCommands.includes(bin) is always false and every command is rejected before execution. commandArgs is parsed by tokenizeArgs and passed to tinyexec's x(bin, commandArgs), which execs argv directly (no shell), so there is no metacharacter-injection surface beyond the intended command execution itself. Whatever the operator allows via ALLOWED_COMMANDS is a deployment decision, not a caller-exploitable gap.

query is spliced unescaped into a query string on a fixed https://pure.md/search host (no encodeURIComponent, so a caller could smuggle extra query parameters into that one fixed-host request), but there is no path by which query can change the target host, so this is not SSRF -- at worst it lets a caller add parameters to the local server's own request to pure.md's own search endpoint.

url is spliced into the path of a fixed https://pure.md/ host (fetch(`https://pure.md/${url}`)); the string concatenation keeps pure.md as the actual fetch target no matter what url contains, since it is appended after the fixed origin rather than replacing it. pure.md's own backend service is an intentional arbitrary-URL-to-markdown reader (its documented product purpose) -- the actual arbitrary-URL fetch happens on pure.md's infrastructure, not this local server's, so this local code has no SSRF surface of its own.
